problem: It says POST is the only common method that is neither safe nor idempotent, but the methods table and the Q7 answer both say PATCH is also neither safe nor idempotent. This internal contradiction will confuse a student who is asked to list the unsafe, non-idempotent methods.
fix: POST and PATCH are the common methods that are neither safe nor idempotent. Retrying a POST after a timeout can create a duplicate order; PATCH may also give a different result when repeated. Retrying PUT or DELETE cannot create a duplicate.

problem: The chapter treats GET, HEAD and OPTIONS as the complete set of safe methods. Standard definitions (RFC 9110) also define TRACE as safe, so a student who writes TRACE in an exam would also be right.
fix: Say: the safe methods in this table are GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; the standard also defines TRACE as safe, and it is rarely used in app code.

problem: "an Angular HTTP client call (Unit 5) all send GET" is wrong: Angular's HttpClient sends whichever method you call, and http.post sends POST.
"The message is plain text" is only true for HTTP/1.1. Section 4 later says HTTP/2 is binary on the wire, so the two statements appear to contradict each other.
fix: "In HTTP/1.1 the message is plain text (ASCII headers); HTTP/2 sends the same information in a binary frame format, covered in Section 4."

problem: The output block prints three loose numbers (84, 0, 3), but part (c) only asks for the two body lengths; the count "3" comes from step 5, which answers a question that was never asked. The output also does not match the parts (a) and (b).
fix: Either add "(d) how many of the replies are 2xx?" to the question, or drop step 5 and the third output line. Label the output lines: GET body = 84 bytes, DELETE body = 0 bytes.

problem: It repeats Worked example 1 almost word for word (same URL, same 200/201/204, same 84 bytes), so it adds no new practice.
fix: Replace it with a different case, for example a 301 redirect with a Location header, or a PUT returning 204, so the student practises a 3xx class and a body-less success.

problem: "gRPC and GraphQL both sit on HTTP/2 framing" is inaccurate: gRPC requires HTTP/2, but GraphQL is transport-agnostic and is most often sent as an ordinary HTTP POST, frequently over HTTP/1.1.
fix: "gRPC requires HTTP/2 framing; GraphQL is transport-agnostic but is usually sent as a single POST to one endpoint, so the methods and status codes still apply."

problem: The sentences "Only a few universities teach HTTP/3 here" and "Only a few universities teach these here" are syllabus-coverage markers repeated inside technical paragraphs. They break the flow and read as filler.
fix: Delete both sentences. If coverage notes are needed, keep one at the end of the section in a single consistent form.
